{{DISPLAYTITLE:Symmetry that can differ from place to place}}
{{Noether's theorems map}}

''Mathematical counterpart: [[Noether's theorems/Second theorem/Groups depending on arbitrary functions|Groups depending on arbitrary functions]].''

Noether's second theorem takes a different kind of symmetry from the first. This
page says what kind, and separates it from two things it gets confused with.

== One clock, or a clock each ==

Give a class of thirty students one stopwatch between them and a shared signal.
Everyone starts at the same moment. If the experiment they are timing does not
care what that moment was, you have a symmetry — the kind on
[[Noether's theorems/Explainers/What a continuous symmetry is|the earlier page]].
One knob: when the signal went.

Now give every student their own stopwatch and let each start whenever they like.
Thirty different starting times. Then a hundred students. Then a student at every
point of the room, so that "when did you start" is answered not by a list of
numbers but by a picture — a value at every location, which you can draw however
you please.

If the physics still comes out the same, you have the second kind of symmetry.
Physicists call it a '''local''' symmetry, because the choice is made afresh at
each place, and a symmetry of the first kind '''global''', because one choice
covers everything.

== A hundred knobs is not the same as a free choice ==

This is where the distinction usually gets blurred, so it is worth being blunt.

Adding more knobs to a global symmetry never turns it into a local one. Thirty
students with thirty stopwatches still gives you thirty numbers. A thousand
students gives you a thousand. However many you add, you are still handing over a
list.

A local symmetry hands over a '''shape'''. You are not picking numbers off a
list; you are drawing a curve, and any curve will do.

Noether is explicit about this. She puts the case of infinitely many numbers in
between the two, as its own category, and notes that her '''first''' theorem
still applies to it. Her second theorem does not. Infinitely many numbers is not
what the second theorem needs.

Why does the difference matter so much? Because of one move the proof makes. With
a free shape, you can choose it to be busy in the middle of a region and to fade
to nothing near the edges. A number cannot do that. A number is the same
everywhere by definition. That one move is what the second theorem's proof turns
on, and it is unavailable no matter how many numbers you have.

== How fussy is the rule ==

There is one more thing to count.

Some rules care only about your choice. Others care about how quickly your choice
changes from one place to the next — and some care about how quickly that rate
changes, and so on.

Noether keeps track of how far this goes, and the answer feeds straight into the
theorem's output. A rule that cares only about the choice gives a simpler result
than one that cares about how the choice varies.

So the theorem needs two counts: how many free shapes there are, and how deep the
rule looks into how they vary. The first fixes how many results come back. The
second fixes how complicated each one is.

== Two examples, and one warning ==

Noether gives two before she proves anything, which is a habit worth copying.

'''Tracing a curve.''' Draw a curve on paper. You can describe it by saying where
you are at each moment as you trace it — but you were free to trace it fast, slow,
or with a pause halfway. The curve is the same. Your freedom to choose the pace is
a free shape, and it is a local symmetry.

'''Choosing coordinates.''' In general relativity you are free to label the points
of spacetime however you like, and you can relabel differently here than there.
Same freedom, one shape for each dimension.

'''The warning.''' It is easy to come away thinking the second theorem is about
general relativity. It is not. Noether names general relativity as an example of a
theory with this kind of symmetry, and near the end of her paper she constructs
another such symmetry with nothing physical attached to it at all, precisely to
show that the physics was never the point.

== Where this goes ==

Every force in modern physics is described by a theory with a local symmetry.
That was not known in 1918 — the idea arrived in the 1950s. The second theorem was
waiting for it.

What it says about such theories is on
[[Noether's theorems/Explainers/The second theorem, and why it is not the first|the
next page]], and the answer is not a conservation law.
